File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "1a4afce34918bdc74ae3f31edaffffaa0ee074d83618f53edfd88137927340b8", "b0cefb66b953e5184b6adb3035e9e267335ac5eabfe1848e07834777b9397b74", "e7347d90653efc565f03733a95e9209d78f9cfa81e31ff2b2dd9d48d75a4b8b1", "558b09d7ad0d1660e2a0fb8a06da81a6f42e06d2", "ba642fe2c7c65e42dd7f6444b83023dc6827e08c"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026 World Cup: Discussing The World’s Biggest Game’s Attack Surface

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-05-28 13 use cases 6 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

The 2026 World Cup presents major cyber risks from ransomware groups, state-aligned actors, and other groups targeting critical infrastructure. Learn more here. The post 2026 World Cup: Discussing The World’s Biggest Game’s Attack Surface appeared first on Unit 42 .

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002 T1219 T1486 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] World Cup 2026 themed lookalike / typosquat domain resolution by corporate hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] NoName057(16) DDoSia client check-in (/client/login, /client/get_targets) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
NoName057(16) DDoSia client check-in (/client/login, /client/get_targets) AICommand & Control High
Hunts for the Russian-aligned NoName057(16) DDoSia botnet client beaconing to its C2 panel. The DDoSia Go-binary uses two distinctive REST URIs to register and pull targeting (/client/login then /client/get_targets) and defaults to the Go-http-client/1.1 user-agent. Catches an infected corporate host being conscripted into hacktivist DDoS against host-city, federation or ticketing infrastructure during the tournament window. Rationale: Anchored on the publicly documented DDoSia client URI scheme (/client/login, /client/get_targets, /client/post_solved) and Go-http-client default UA. The article names NoName057(16) and references their 3,700+ DDoS attacks against NATO targets through 2026; cross-referenced with Sekoia and NCSC public reporting on DDoSia client internals. Article: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/fifa-world-cup-attack-surface/ Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/following-noname05716-ddosia-projects-targets/ • https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/news/joint-advisory-russia-aligned-noname05716 • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1023/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1498 T1583.003
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SaaS APIs that happen to use /client/login REST routes (some IdP/SDK auth endpoints)
  • Internal Go-written services calling internal REST APIs with similar URI naming
  • Pentest/red-team simulating DDoSia C2 for tabletop exercises
  • Researchers/threat intel teams interacting with sinkholed DDoSia infrastructure
  • Mobile app SDKs (Firebase, Sentry) that occasionally use /client/* URIs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com", "atlassian.com", "gitlab.com", "microsoft.com", "firebase", "sentry.io")) and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msedge.exe", "chrome.exe", "firefox.exe") and array_length(URIs) == 1)
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source host is a corporate asset; identify the process initiating the requests (DDoSia drops as dosia.exe / Go-compiled binary in %TEMP% or %APPDATA%). Pull SHA256, parent process, and the C2 IP/domain. Cross-check the C2 IP against Sekoia and abuse.ch DDoSia trackers. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via EDR; block the C2 IP and domain at proxy/firewall; revoke any cached credentials and browser sessions on the host (DDoSia loaders are often dropped by info-stealers first). Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the C2 IP across NetworkConnect events for sibling beaconing hosts; query DNS for the C2 domain enterprise-wide; check email gateway for inbound lure messages (often game-pirate or crypto-themed lures) in the prior 14 days that match the loader's file hash.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/client/login", "/client/get_targets", "/client/post_solved")
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com", "atlassian.com", "gitlab.com", "microsoft.com"))
| summarize URIs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hits = count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP
| where array_length(URIs) >= 2 or Hits > 5
| order by LastSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/client/login", "/client/get_targets", "/client/post_solved")
| where not (Url has_any ("github.com", "atlassian.com", "gitlab.com", "microsoft.com"))
| summarize URIs = make_set(Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(), UAs = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| where array_length(URIs) >= 2 or Hits > 5
| order by LastSeen desc
title: DDoSia (NoName057-16) C2 Check-in URI Pattern
id: 7f3a8b2e-1c44-4f67-89ab-cdef01234567
description: Detects NoName057(16) DDoSia client check-in via the /client/login and /client/get_targets REST endpoints used by the Go-based botnet client
references:

tags:

detection:

      - '/client/get_targets'
      - '/client/post_solved'
  selection_ua:

| count>0

World Cup 2026 themed lookalike / typosquat domain resolution by corporate hosts AIDelivery Medium
Hunting query for corporate endpoints resolving newly-observed domains containing FIFA / World Cup 2026 / Hayya / FanID keyword variants — the article cites 16,000+ scam domains observed in Qatar 2022 and forecasts the same pattern at scale across the 16 host cities. Catches credential-harvest landing pages, fake ticket-resale sites, and fraudulent fan-portal lookalikes used in the run-up to and during the tournament window (June 11 – July 19, 2026). Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit forecast of typosquat/lookalike domains targeting fans — directly references Group-IB's 16,000+ scam domains from Qatar 2022 and the five categories of ticket-themed fraud. The regex covers the keyword roots (fifa, worldcup, hayya, fanid) that scam domains pivot on. Article: https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/fifa-world-cup-attack-surface/ Cross-checked against: • https://www.group-ib.com/blog/qatar-2022/ • https://www.fifa.com/tournaments/mens/worldcup/canadamexicousa2026
ATT&CKT1583.001 T1566.002 T1598.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate sponsor / merchandise / news domains that include 'worldcup' or 'fifa' tokens (e.g. fan blogs, betting affiliates with proper licensing)
  • Corporate marketing campaigns where the org is an official sponsor and registers themed campaign domains
  • Internal sandbox detonations of phishing samples that trigger DNS for the lookalike
  • Security teams testing URL filtering against newly-registered domains
  • Employees browsing news coverage on legitimate domains that embed third-party ad/tracking lookalikes
Suppression filter
| where not (domain has_any ("sponsor.fifa.com", "news.", "blog.", "betting", "odds")) and not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("outlook.exe") and DeviceCount < 3)
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: bucket new domains by first-seen, run WHOIS for registration age (anything <30 days at tournament time is high-suspicion); confirm whether the host actually resolved/loaded the page (cross-check proxy HTTP logs); check if a credential-harvest form was submitted. Step 2 — Contain: add the domain to DNS/proxy blocklist enterprise-wide; if any user submitted credentials, force password reset + MFA re-enrolment and revoke active sessions; pull email gateway logs for inbound messages linking to the domain. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the NS / hosting IP for sibling domains registered by the same actor (campaigns register in clusters of 50-200); search DNS for any of those siblings; alert IT comms to warn staff about the active lure theme.
let LookalikeRegex = @"(?i)(fifa|world.?cup.?2026|wc.?2026|hayya|fan.?id)";
let LegitTLDs = dynamic(["fifa.com", "fifaworldcup.com", "hayya.qa", "hayya.com", "fifamuseum.com", "ussoccer.com", "canadasoccer.com", "miseleccion.mx"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex LookalikeRegex
| extend domain = tostring(split(RemoteUrl, "/")[2])
| where not (LegitTLDs has_any (domain)) and not (domain endswith "fifa.com" or domain endswith "fifaworldcup.com" or domain endswith "hayya.qa")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), DeviceCount = dcount(DeviceName), SampleProc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), SampleHost = any(DeviceName) by domain
| where DeviceCount < 50
| order by FirstSeen desc
let LookalikeRegex = @"(?i)(fifa|world.?cup.?2026|wc.?2026|hayya|fan.?id)";
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DnsQuery matches regex LookalikeRegex
| where not (DnsQuery endswith "fifa.com" or DnsQuery endswith "fifaworldcup.com" or DnsQuery endswith "hayya.qa" or DnsQuery endswith "hayya.com" or DnsQuery endswith "ussoccer.com" or DnsQuery endswith "canadasoccer.com")
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), HostCount = dcount(SrcHostname), SampleSrc = any(SrcIpAddr) by DnsQuery
| where HostCount < 50
| order by FirstSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized axios npm package postinstall: node.exe spawned from plain-crypto-js dependency · [LLM] axios RAT Windows persistence: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe drop + %TEMP%\6202033.vbs/.ps1 staging
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] axios RAT C2 callout to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Trojanized axios npm package postinstall: node.exe spawned from plain-crypto-js dependency AIInstallation High
Hunts the postinstall hook of the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 dependency that ESET-mentioned trojanized axios versions (1.14.1, 0.30.4) silently pulled in. The malicious package's only purpose is to run `node setup.js` from its install folder, which then fetches a platform-specific RAT from C2. plain-crypto-js is never imported by axios source and is never a legitimate transitive dep. Rationale: plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 is the never-legitimate dependency injected by the trojanized axios versions; its postinstall fires `node setup.js`. Anchoring on the exact package name (case-sensitive on npm — always lowercase) gives near-zero FPs while catching every infected build host. Cross-checked against StepSecurity, Microsoft, Sophos, Datadog Security Labs and the axios GitHub post-mortem. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/10636 • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/north-korea-threat-actor-targets-axios-npm-package
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher detonating the malicious package in a sandbox to write detections
  • SCA / dep-vuln scanner (Snyk, socket.dev, Mend) re-resolving lockfiles that still pin the bad version
  • Developer running `npm audit` against an old lockfile that lists plain-crypto-js
  • Mirror / proxy registry (Verdaccio, Nexus) replaying postinstalls during cache validation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\socket-cli\", @"\snyk\", @"\npm-audit\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm audit", "snyk test", "socket scan"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pivot to the host's package-manager footprint (npm/yarn/pnpm logs, .npm cache, project package-lock.json) and confirm axios was resolved at 1.14.1 or 0.30.4 around 2026-03-31 00:21–03:15 UTC. Identify the developer / build-pipeline identity that triggered the install. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, rotate all credentials, tokens and SSH/CI secrets that ever sat in env vars on it, kill any wt.exe / ld.py / com.apple.act.mond child processes, and force-pin axios to 1.14.0 / 0.30.3 across the org's lockfiles. Step 3 — Hunt: search all build agents and dev workstations for the C2 indicators (sfrclak.com, 142.11.206.73:8000) and for the persistence artifacts (UC2). Pull the host's outbound traffic for the 24h after install for staged credential exfil to packages.npm.org/product[012] paths.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where (FileName =~ "node.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
   or FolderPath has @"\node_modules\plain-crypto-js\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "node.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "node.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
   or TargetProcessCommandLine has "plain-crypto-js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          ParentName = ActingProcessName, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildName = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Trojanized axios npm package - plain-crypto-js postinstall execution
id: 5c8b1f2a-7e4d-4d8a-9c2b-3f0a8e1b6d72
status: experimental
description: Detects node.exe execution referencing the malicious plain-crypto-js dependency injected by the trojanized axios versions 1.14.1 and 0.30.4 (npm supply chain compromise, 2026-03-31).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/eset-apt-activity-report-q4-2025-q1-2026/
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
  - https://github.com/axios/axios/issues/10636
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/29
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.execution
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith: '\node.exe'
  selection_anchor:
    CommandLine|contains: 'plain-crypto-js'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_anchor
falsepositives:
  - Security research sandboxing the malicious package for analysis
  - Vulnerability scanner emulating the postinstall hook (e.g. socket.dev, Snyk)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe OR *\\NODE.EXE) @CommandLine:*plain-crypto-js*
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i CommandLine=/plain-crypto-js/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

axios RAT Windows persistence: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe drop + %TEMP%\6202033.vbs/.ps1 staging AIInstallation High
Hunts the Windows-specific file artifacts dropped by the second-stage RAT delivered through the trojanized axios npm packages. The dropper writes %TEMP%\6202033.vbs and %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 as staging, then persists as %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe — note that legitimate Windows Terminal wt.exe lives in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Microsoft\WindowsApps, NOT ProgramData, so the path itself is the discriminator. Rationale: Three high-specificity anchors from corroborated incident write-ups: %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe (Windows Terminal never installs there — it's in WindowsApps), %TEMP%\6202033.vbs and %TEMP%\6202033.ps1 (the C2 server id 6202033 is hard-coded in the dropper, so the filename literal is the IOC). The WindowsApps exclusion stops the only obvious FP path. Verified against StepSecurity, Datadog Security Labs, Sophos. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-to-deploy-malware • https://www.elastic.co/security-labs/axios-one-rat-to-rule-them-all
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1059.001 T1059.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft Store reinstalling Windows Terminal under a non-standard path on a heavily customised image
  • SCCM / Intune package that genuinely stages a renamed wt.exe in ProgramData (uncommon — verify owner)
  • Forensic tooling that copies artifacts into TEMP for analysis using a numeric ticket ID that happens to be 6202033
  • Backup or imaging product that round-trips the previously-dropped wt.exe out of quarantine
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("taskhostw.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","msiexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "userinit.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the writing process from InitiatingProcessFileName — expected chain is node.exe -> wscript.exe / powershell.exe writing the VBS/PS1, then VBS dropping wt.exe. Pull the SHA256 of wt.exe and submit to VT / Falcon Intelligence. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill the wt.exe and any persistence (Run keys, Scheduled Tasks, Services) pointing at it, quarantine all three files, rotate credentials of any user logged on during the install. Step 3 — Hunt: query DeviceNetworkEvents from the same host for connections to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 (UC3); query the org for any other host that resolved sfrclak.com in the last 60 days even if no file artifact landed; review npm install history for axios 1.14.1 / 0.30.4.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(60d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where (FileName =~ "wt.exe" and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\" and not(FolderPath has @"\WindowsApps\"))
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where (TargetFileName =~ "wt.exe" and TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\" and TargetFilePath !has @"\WindowsApps\")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^6202033\.(vbs|ps1)$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername,
          TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
          ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

axios RAT C2 callout to sfrclak.com / 142.11.206.73:8000 AICommand & Control High
Hunts the dedicated C2 infrastructure of the second-stage RAT delivered via the trojanized axios npm packages. The dropper beacons to http://sfrclak.com:8000/6202033 to fetch platform-specific payloads, then POSTs back to packages.npm.org/product0|1|2 (note: the registry domain is spoofed in the URI path, the actual hostname is sfrclak.com). The IP 142.11.206.73 and port 8000 give a clean network-only fallback when DNS isn't logged. Rationale: sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73:8000 are the dedicated, never-legitimate C2 for the axios RAT campaign — confirmed across StepSecurity, Microsoft, Sophos and Datadog Security Labs incident write-ups. Joining domain + IP + port covers the case where the host bypasses DNS (hard-coded IP) and where DNS is the only telemetry available. The 90-day lookback is intentional: the malicious packages were live only ~3 hours but compromised hosts may have beaconed since. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/axios-compromised-on-npm-malicious-versions-drop-remote-access-trojan • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised-to-deploy-malware • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform (MISP, Recorded Future, internal TI scanner) probing the IOC
  • Security researcher reproducing the campaign in a lab segment
  • Web proxy / sandbox detonating sample URLs through corporate egress
  • DNS sinkhole that resolves but does not block — generates a query event with sinkhole RR data
  • WAF / SIEM enrichment job doing reverse-DNS lookups against the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","curl.exe","misp-modules.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\TI-Enrichment\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull InitiatingProcessFileName for every beacon — legitimate beacons should be browsers from researchers; suspicious beacons will be node.exe, wscript.exe, powershell.exe, or %PROGRAMDATA%\wt.exe. Correlate the host to UC1/UC2 hits in the prior 24h. Step 2 — Contain: block sfrclak.com and 142.11.206.73 at the perimeter and DNS, isolate any matching host, rotate all secrets accessible from it. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFolderPath for other node_modules paths to find sibling-compromised packages; query the entire fleet for resolutions of sfrclak.com going back 90 days; review egress proxy logs for POSTs to URI path patterns /product0, /product1, /product2 since those are the platform-tagged exfil endpoints even when the Host header is spoofed.
let C2Domain = dynamic(["sfrclak.com"]);
let C2IP = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(90d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2IP)
   or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domain)
   or (RemoteIP in (C2IP) and RemotePort == 8000)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Domain = dynamic(["sfrclak.com"]);
let C2IP = dynamic(["142.11.206.73"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DstIpAddr in (C2IP) or DstHostname in~ (C2Domain) or Url has "sfrclak.com"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url, SrcUsername),
(ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
   | where DnsQuery has "sfrclak.com"
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

let LookbackDays = 7d;

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")

DeviceFileEvents

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Pirates in the crosshairs: how one cybercrime gang has been infecting book, movi
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] HLS Installer.874.exe DLL side-load from pirate-streaming ZIP lure · [LLM] SilentCryptoMiner-fork: Defender exclusions added for %USERPROFILE%, %PROGRAMDATA%, %WINDIR%, .exe, .dll · [LLM] MSRT tampering: HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\MRT DontOfferThroughWUAU = 1 · [LLM] powercfg sleep/hibernate disable burst (4-command sequence) · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SilentCryptoMiner DNS tunneling to *.microsoft.com lookalike and known C2 .space domains · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains · DNS tunneling / TXT-heavy domain queries
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
HLS Installer.874.exe DLL side-load from pirate-streaming ZIP lure AIInstallation High
Hunts the SilentCryptoMiner-fork delivery chain: the bundled legitimate 'HLS Installer.874.exe' executes from a user-downloaded archive and loads a same-directory rogue DLL, which then reflectively maps the encrypted main module. Targets the exact binary name and the user-writable parent folders (Downloads / Temp / Desktop) the lure ZIP unpacks into. Rationale: Anchors on the article's verbatim binary name 'HLS Installer.874.exe' (code block 1) and the user-writable archive-unpack locations where pirated lures land. Defender query joins process-create to image-load on the same PID to confirm side-loading rather than just an executed installer. Cross-checked NTT Security's 'chromium-patch-nightly' lure variant referenced in the article body. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1574/002/ • https://github.com/SilentMine/SilentCryptoMiner
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate HLS-related video-tooling installers a user genuinely downloaded from a vendor
  • Penetration-test side-loading lab work mirroring this campaign
  • Repackaged streaming utilities downloaded from forums but not malicious
  • Security-research detonation of the sample in a controlled host
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Microsoft", "Apple", "Google")) and InitiatingProcessTokenElevation != "TokenElevationTypeDefault"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the parent process and the source URL of the ZIP from DeviceFileEvents.FileOriginUrl/FileOriginReferrerUrl; hash the side-loaded DLL and check against IOC MD5s 6a0fe6065d76715feebc1526d456db73 / 7f624407ae489324e96a708a09c17e6f / 02a43b3423367b9dddc24cc7dfc070df. 2) Contain: isolate the device, quarantine the EXE+DLL pair under the unpack directory, kill any descendant miner processes. 3) Hunt: pivot on the DLL SHA256 across the fleet, search DNS for the article's .space C2 domains and the IP 107.172.212.235, look for the powercfg hibernate-disable commands and Defender exclusion additions described in the other UCs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "HLS Installer.874.exe"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HLS Installer.874.exe"
    | where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\")
    | where FileName endswith ".dll"
) on DeviceId, $left.ProcessId == $right.InitiatingProcessId
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessFolder=FolderPath, ProcessCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SideLoadedDll=FileName1, DllFolder=FolderPath1, DllSha256=SHA2561
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 14d;
let ProcEvts = ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "HLS Installer.874.exe"
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Desktop\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\");
let DllEvts = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "HLS Installer.874.exe"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll";
ProcEvts
| join kind=inner (DllEvts) on DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HLS Installer.874.exe Execution From User-Writable Path
id: c93f5b62-3a17-4f4a-9f1d-8c0f47b8ab21
description: Detects execution of the legitimately-signed 'HLS Installer.874.exe' binary used as a DLL side-loading host by the SilentCryptoMiner-fork distributed via pirated streaming and digital-library sites.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/video-books-pirates-miners-rat/119943/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/28
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\HLS Installer.874.exe'
  paths:
    Image|contains:
      - '\Downloads\'
      - '\Desktop\'
      - '\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\Local\Temp\'
  condition: selection and paths
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) @Image:(*\HLS\ Installer.874.exe OR *\hls\ installer.874.exe OR *\HLS\ INSTALLER.874.EXE) (@Image:*\Downloads\* OR @Image:*\Desktop\* OR @Image:*\Temp\* OR @Image:*\AppData\Local\Temp\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\HLS Installer\.874\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\(Downloads|Desktop|Temp|AppData\\\\Local\\\\Temp)\\\\", field=ImageFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT

SilentCryptoMiner-fork: Defender exclusions added for %USERPROFILE%, %PROGRAMDATA%, %WINDIR%, .exe, .dll AIInstallation High
Detects the privileged preparatory step in the SilentCryptoMiner-fork chain: bulk addition of Defender path AND extension exclusions covering EXE, DLL, and the three root profile directories. The combination is unusual outside MDM / GPO baselines and is the campaign's defense-evasion fingerprint. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact exclusion targets (.exe, .dll, %USERPROFILE%, %PROGRAMDATA%, %WINDIR%). Requiring >=3 of the five exclusion strings within a 10-min window distinguishes the campaign's bulk-add behaviour from a single legitimate IT exclusion. Cross-checked MITRE T1562.001 and prior SilentCryptoMiner write-ups (Kaspersky 'Undercover miner' post referenced inline in the article). Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001/ • https://securelist.com/silentcryptominer-as-restriction-bypass-tool/115960/
ATT&CKT1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-management tools (SCCM/Intune/JAMF) applying corporate AV exclusion baselines
  • Security software installers (other AV products) adding their own paths
  • Developer setting up a build-server exclusion path for self-signed binaries
  • Backup software (Veeam, Acronis) registering exclusion paths
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe", "MpCmdRun.exe", "ConfigSecurityPolicy.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "CcmEval.exe", "sense.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName — corporate MDM/Intune agents and ConfigMgr will appear here legitimately; anything else writing to Exclusions is suspect. Pull the exclusion set and look for the article's signature combo (.exe + .dll + %USERPROFILE%). 2) Contain: remove the malicious exclusions via Set-MpPreference -Remove, isolate the host, kill any process running from the now-excluded paths. 3) Hunt: pivot on the InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet; cross-correlate with the MSRT-tamper, powercfg, and DNS-tunneling UCs in this pack — the campaign chains all four.
let WindowMins = 10m;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions"
| where RegistryValueName in~ (".exe", ".dll") or RegistryValueName has_any ("%USERPROFILE%", "%PROGRAMDATA%", "%WINDIR%")
| summarize ExclusionCount = dcount(RegistryValueName), Exclusions = make_set(RegistryValueName), Bucket = bin(Timestamp, WindowMins), Actor = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), ActorCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceId, DeviceName
| where ExclusionCount >= 3
| order by Bucket desc
let WindowMins = 10m;
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions"
| where RegistryValue in~ (".exe", ".dll") or RegistryValue has_any ("%USERPROFILE%", "%PROGRAMDATA%", "%WINDIR%")
| summarize ExclusionCount = dcount(RegistryValue), Exclusions = make_set(RegistryValue), Bucket = bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMins), Actor = any(ActingProcessName), ActorCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by DvcHostname
| where ExclusionCount >= 3
| order by Bucket desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.defender) @EventID:13 (@TargetObject:*\Microsoft\Windows\ Defender\Exclusions\Paths\* OR @TargetObject:*\Microsoft\Windows\ Defender\Exclusions\Extensions\*) (@TargetObject:*%USERPROFILE%* OR @TargetObject:*%PROGRAMDATA%* OR @TargetObject:*%WINDIR%* OR @TargetObject:*\.exe OR @TargetObject:*\.dll)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| regex("\\\\Microsoft\\\\Windows Defender\\\\Exclusions\\\\(Paths|Extensions)", field=RegObjectName)
| (RegValueName=/%USERPROFILE%/i OR RegValueName=/%PROGRAMDATA%/i OR RegValueName=/%WINDIR%/i OR RegValueName=/^\.exe$/i OR RegValueName=/^\.dll$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=RegValueName, distinct=true, as=ExclusionCount))
| ExclusionCount >= 3
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where (Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Exclusions\\Paths\\*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Exclusions\\Extensions\\*") (Registry.registry_value_name="*%USERPROFILE%*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*%PROGRAMDATA%*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*%WINDIR%*" OR Registry.registry_value_name=".exe" OR Registry.registry_value_name=".dll") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.process_name Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | stats values(registry_value_name) as exclusions dc(registry_value_name) as exclusion_count min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by dest user process_name | where exclusion_count >= 3
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where (Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Exclusions\\Paths\\*" OR Registry.registry_path="*\\Microsoft\\Windows Defender\\Exclusions\\Extensions\\*") (Registry.registry_value_name="*%USERPROFILE%*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*%PROGRAMDATA%*" OR Registry.registry_value_name="*%WINDIR%*" OR Registry.registry_value_name=".exe" OR Registry.registry_value_name=".dll") by Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.process_name Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | stats values(registry_value_name) as exclusions dc(registry_value_name) as exclusion_count min(firstTime) as firstTime max(lastTime) as lastTime by dest user process_name | where exclusion_count >= 3
MSRT tampering: HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\MRT DontOfferThroughWUAU = 1 AIInstallation High
Detects the SilentCryptoMiner-fork's MSRT-suppression step: writing the DontOfferThroughWUAU=1 policy value under HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\MRT to block reinstallation, often paired with deletion of %WINDIR%\System32\mrt.exe via ZwSetInformationFile FileDispositionInformation. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact policy path 'HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\MRT', value name 'DontOfferThroughWUAU', and the data value 1 used to block MSRT reinstall via Windows Update. Pairs the registry write with the article-described mrt.exe deletion under System32 (via ZwSetInformationFile/FileDispositionInformation) for higher fidelity. Cross-checked MITRE T1562.001 mapping. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1562/001/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/ntifs/nf-ntifs-zwsetinformationfile
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT admin applying a corporate GPO that intentionally suppresses MSRT delivery (rare, usually scripted on a fleet)
  • Image-build / golden-image preparation script disabling MSRT before sysprep
  • Third-party patch-management product (e.g. Ivanti, ManageEngine) toggling WSUS-related policies
  • Legitimate WSUS migration script enumerating policy keys
Suppression filter
| where not(Actor in~ ("svchost.exe", "gpscript.exe", "gpupdate.exe", "WmiPrvSE.exe")) and not(ActorCmd has "GroupPolicy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName — legitimate GPO writes come from GPSVC / WmiPrvSE; anything else (especially a side-loaded user-mode process) is high-confidence malicious. Confirm whether mrt.exe was also deleted (FileHit branch). 2) Contain: re-enable MRT by deleting the DontOfferThroughWUAU value, isolate the device, restore mrt.exe from a clean image, force a Defender update. 3) Hunt: pivot on the writing process SHA256, look for the Defender-exclusion UC and powercfg hibernate-disable UC on the same host within +/-10 minutes — they're the same chain.
let Lookback = 14d;
let RegHit = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet", "RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Policies\Microsoft\MRT"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "DontOfferThroughWUAU"
| where tostring(RegistryValueData) in ("1", "0x1", "0x00000001")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Signal="MRT_PolicyReg";
let FileHit = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where ActionType in ("FileDeleted", "FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\System32\" and FileName =~ "mrt.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Actor=InitiatingProcessFileName, ActorCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Signal="MRT_FileDelete";
union RegHit, FileHit
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 14d;
let RegHit = ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Software\Policies\Microsoft\MRT"
| where RegistryValue =~ "DontOfferThroughWUAU"
| where tostring(RegistryValueData) in ("1", "0x1", "0x00000001")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Actor=ActingProcessName, ActorCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine, Signal="MRT_PolicyReg";
let FileHit = ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where EventType in ("FileDeleted", "FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has @"\System32\"
| where TargetFileName =~ "mrt.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, Actor=ActingProcessName, ActorCmd=ActingProcessCommandLine, Signal="MRT_FileDelete";
union RegHit, FileHit
| order by TimeGenerated desc

powercfg sleep/hibernate disable burst (4-command sequence) AIInstallation High
Detects the SilentCryptoMiner-fork's miner-uptime preparation: four powercfg commands disabling hibernate AC, hibernate DC, standby AC, and standby DC in rapid succession. The four-command burst from a single non-administrative parent is the campaign signature distinguishing miners from legitimate power-management tweaks. Rationale: Anchors on the four verbatim powercfg arguments from the article (table 2: hibernate-timeout-ac/dc, standby-timeout-ac/dc, all set to 0). Requiring >=3 distinct variants in a 5-min window separates the miner's burst from a sysadmin tweaking a single setting. The /x form in the article is also alternative-matched. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1496/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/device-experiences/powercfg-command-line-options
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Laptop-power-profile tuning by IT during desktop standardisation
  • Kiosk / digital-signage build script disabling all sleep states
  • Citrix/VDI gold-image preparation scripts
  • Mining-rig-like legitimate workloads (rendering farm, ML training boxes) configured by their owners
Suppression filter
| where not(Parent in~ ("gpscript.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "MsSense.exe", "sysprep.exe", "setupcl.exe")) and not(ParentCmd has_any ("GroupPolicy", "Intune", "ConfigMgr"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the parent process — Group Policy / SCCM /Intune scripts are legitimate; user-shell or unknown binaries running this from %TEMP%/%USERPROFILE% are not. Pull the parent SHA256. 2) Contain: re-enable power-saving with the corporate profile, isolate if the parent is unsigned/untrusted, kill any high-CPU processes running from user-writable paths. 3) Hunt: cross-correlate with the Defender-exclusion and MSRT-tamper UCs on the same host within +/-15 minutes; pivot on parent process SHA256 across the fleet and search for outbound traffic to 107.172.212.235 or the .space C2 domains.
let WindowMins = 5m;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "powercfg.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-hibernate-timeout-ac 0", "-hibernate-timeout-dc 0", "-standby-timeout-ac 0", "-standby-timeout-dc 0", "/x -hibernate-timeout", "/x -standby-timeout")
| extend Flag = case(
    ProcessCommandLine has "hibernate-timeout-ac", "hib_ac",
    ProcessCommandLine has "hibernate-timeout-dc", "hib_dc",
    ProcessCommandLine has "standby-timeout-ac", "sby_ac",
    ProcessCommandLine has "standby-timeout-dc", "sby_dc",
    "other")
| summarize Variants = dcount(Flag), Cmds = make_set(ProcessCommandLine), Parent = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), ParentCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), Bucket = bin(Timestamp, WindowMins) by DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName
| where Variants >= 3
| order by Bucket desc
let WindowMins = 5m;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "powercfg.exe"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-hibernate-timeout-ac 0", "-hibernate-timeout-dc 0", "-standby-timeout-ac 0", "-standby-timeout-dc 0", "/x -hibernate-timeout", "/x -standby-timeout")
| extend Flag = case(
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "hibernate-timeout-ac", "hib_ac",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "hibernate-timeout-dc", "hib_dc",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "standby-timeout-ac", "sby_ac",
    ActingProcessCommandLine has "standby-timeout-dc", "sby_dc",
    "other")
| summarize Variants = dcount(Flag), Cmds = make_set(ActingProcessCommandLine), Parent = any(ParentProcessName), ParentCmd = any(ParentProcessCommandLine), Bucket = bin(TimeGenerated, WindowMins) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername
| where Variants >= 3
| order by Bucket desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) @EventID:(1 OR 4688) (@Image:*\powercfg.exe OR @Image:*\POWERCFG.EXE) (@CommandLine:*-hibernate-timeout-ac\ 0* OR @CommandLine:*-hibernate-timeout-dc\ 0* OR @CommandLine:*-standby-timeout-ac\ 0* OR @CommandLine:*-standby-timeout-dc\ 0*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\\powercfg\.exe$/i
| regex("-(hibernate|standby)-timeout-(ac|dc)\\s+0", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count(field=CommandLine, distinct=true, as=Variants))
| Variants >= 3

SilentCryptoMiner DNS tunneling to *.microsoft.com lookalike and known C2 .space domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts the article's specific C2 channel: DNS queries to lookalike domains ending in 'microsoft.com' but resolving to non-Microsoft IPs, plus direct queries to the article's six .space/.online IOC domains. The DNS-tunneled fingerprint payload (CPU info, C: serial, elevation flag, start time) is encoded into a single large subdomain label. Rationale: Anchors on the article's eight IOC domains, the IP 107.172.212.235, and the described DNS-tunneling pattern of long subdomain labels under *.microsoft.com whose A-record resolution falls outside Microsoft's published ranges. The query unions the high-confidence IOC branch with the heuristic tunneling branch so legacy unsubmitted-IP detections and known-IOC detections share one rule. Cross-checked MITRE T1071.004 / T1572 mappings. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/004/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/enterprise/urls-and-ip-address-ranges
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Microsoft Edge / Office DNS queries to obscure microsoft.com subdomains during product telemetry
  • Long DNS queries by Microsoft Defender ASR/MAPS to *.microsoft.com edge nodes (different IP range)
  • Threat-intel sandbox detonations of the sample inside the corporate network
  • An MS partner CDN node briefly resolved to a non-MS range during a DNS infra failover
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","OfficeClickToRun.exe","MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName — if a non-browser non-MS-signed process is making the resolution, treat as confirmed. Hash the binary and check against the three article MD5s. 2) Contain: sinkhole the eight IOC domains and block 107.172.212.235 at the perimeter; isolate the host; collect a memory image (the main module reflectively loads, so the on-disk DLL alone is insufficient for forensics). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same writing process across the fleet, look back 90 days for the file.ipfs.us.69.mu legacy domain, correlate with the Defender-exclusion / MSRT-tamper / powercfg UCs in this pack — they're the same chain.
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["urush1bar4.online","file.ipfs.us.69.mu","5d14vnfb.space","r7mvjl67.space","zgj1tam9.space","jeaw520i.space","qdmagva5.space","m4yuri.online"]);
let CampaignIp = "107.172.212.235";
let IocHit = DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (isnotempty(RemoteUrl) and RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignDomains)) or RemoteIP == CampaignIp
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, Signal="IOC_Hit";
let TunnelHit = DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse" or ActionType has "Dns"
| where RemoteUrl endswith ".microsoft.com"
| extend QueryLen = strlen(RemoteUrl)
| where QueryLen > 80
| where not(RemoteIP startswith "13." or RemoteIP startswith "20." or RemoteIP startswith "23." or RemoteIP startswith "40." or RemoteIP startswith "52." or RemoteIP startswith "104." or RemoteIP startswith "131.107." or RemoteIP startswith "134.170." or RemoteIP startswith "137.116." or RemoteIP startswith "157.55." or RemoteIP startswith "168.61." or RemoteIP startswith "191.236." or RemoteIP startswith "207.46.")
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, Signal="DNS_Tunnel_MSLookalike";
union IocHit, TunnelHit
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignDomains = dynamic(["urush1bar4.online","file.ipfs.us.69.mu","5d14vnfb.space","r7mvjl67.space","zgj1tam9.space","jeaw520i.space","qdmagva5.space","m4yuri.online"]);
let CampaignIp = "107.172.212.235";
let MsRanges = dynamic(["13.","20.","23.","40.","52.","104.","131.107.","134.170.","137.116.","157.55.","168.61.","191.236.","207.46."]);
let IocHit = ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (CampaignDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr, Signal="IOC_Hit";
let TunnelHit = ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where DnsQuery endswith ".microsoft.com"
| extend QueryLen = strlen(DnsQuery)
| where QueryLen > 80
| extend InMsRange = iff(isnotempty(DstIpAddr) and (DstIpAddr startswith "13." or DstIpAddr startswith "20." or DstIpAddr startswith "23." or DstIpAddr startswith "40." or DstIpAddr startswith "52." or DstIpAddr startswith "104." or DstIpAddr startswith "131.107." or DstIpAddr startswith "134.170." or DstIpAddr startswith "137.116." or DstIpAddr startswith "157.55." or DstIpAddr startswith "168.61." or DstIpAddr startswith "191.236." or DstIpAddr startswith "207.46."), true, false)
| where InMsRange == false
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DstIpAddr, Signal="DNS_Tunnel_MSLookalike";
union IocHit, TunnelHit
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
