title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or SHA1 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or MD5 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c", "2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96", "7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 sighting in file or email telemetry · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] BTMOB C2/phishing domain contact — arbsniper.com · [LLM] Egress to BTMOB hosted C2 cluster (LATAM/Hetzner IPs, Google CDN excluded) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
BTMOB C2/phishing domain contact — arbsniper.com AICommand & Control High
Detects any corporate-managed device (or perimeter proxy) resolving or connecting to arbsniper.com, the only non-CDN domain ESET ties to BTMOB Android RAT infrastructure. Catches infected BYOD on corporate WiFi, Windows endpoints that fetched the phishing lure, and proxy egress. Rationale: arbsniper.com is the single non-CDN C2/phishing domain ESET attributes to BTMOB and is also cited in Cyble's Feb 2025 write-up (https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/) and Malpedia (https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob). Two-source corroboration — high fidelity. The other ESET IPs include Google CDN ranges (74.125.x.x, 142.251.x.x, 173.194.x.x, 192.178.x.x) which would FP catastrophically; this UC pivots on the high-signal domain instead. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/btmob-android-rat-maas-builder/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / TI team manually browsing arbsniper.com from a corporate workstation for analysis
  • Automated sandbox/detonation traffic from an internal CAPE/CuckooFork host
  • DNS sinkhole that intentionally resolves the domain for logging
  • Internet-scanning project (Shodan-style) hitting the IP that happens to host the domain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("ti-analyst","sandbox-svc","detonation-svc") and DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessFileName — if it's a browser, the user clicked a BTMOB lure; if it's a non-browser process (Java, Python, native PE) the host is likely already compromised and beaconing. Check user's recent email/SMS for BTMOB lures impersonating streaming, crypto-mining, or LATAM tax-authority brands (ESET cites Argentina ARCA). 2) Contain: block arbsniper.com at the proxy and DNS; if BYOD/MDM-enrolled, push device-quarantine / force MDM re-enrollment; revoke active SSO/VPN sessions for the user. 3) Hunt: pivot on the user across UrlClickEvents and EmailUrlInfo for related fake-store URLs; sweep DeviceFileEvents and EmailAttachmentInfo for the BTMOB APK SHA256 list (see sibling UC); enumerate other devices that resolved the domain in the last 30 days.
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let BadDomain = "arbsniper.com";
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where RemoteUrl has BadDomain
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let BadDomain = "arbsniper.com";
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where Name has BadDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Host=Computer, ClientIP, Query=Name, Result=Result),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where RequestURL has BadDomain or DestinationHostName has BadDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Source=DeviceVendor, Host=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Query=coalesce(RequestURL, DestinationHostName), Result=DeviceAction),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where DnsQuery has BadDomain
  | project TimeGenerated, Source=EventProduct, Host=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, Result=DnsResponseCodeName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: Detects DNS resolution or network/web request to arbsniper.com, BTMOB Android RAT C2/phishing infrastructure tracked by ESET (April 2026) and Cyble (Feb 2025).
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/malware/btmob-stealthy-rat-burrowing-deep-android-devices/
  - https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/30
tags:
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1583.001
detection:
  selection_dns:
    QueryName|endswith: 'arbsniper.com'
  selection_url:
    Url|contains: 'arbsniper.com'
  selection_dest:
    DestinationHostname|endswith: 'arbsniper.com'
  condition: 1 of selection_*
logsource:
  category: dns
level: high
falsepositives:
  - Threat-intel research traffic to the indicator from a known sandbox/analyst host
  - Web crawlers indexing the BTMOB landing page
(@network.destination.ip:* AND (@dns.question.name:*arbsniper.com OR @url:*arbsniper.com* OR @http.url:*arbsniper.com* OR @DestinationHostname:*arbsniper.com OR @QueryName:*arbsniper.com)) AND source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security OR zeek OR suricata OR proxy OR cloudflare OR cloudtrail)
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/arbsniper\.com$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|outlook|teams)\.exe$/i) | regex("arbsniper\.com", field=DomainName) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(), min(@timestamp, as=firstSeen), max(@timestamp, as=lastSeen)])
NETWORK

BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 sighting in file or email telemetry AIDelivery Medium
Hash-IOC sweep for the BTMOB v2.5+ APK sample corpus published by ESET (cross-referenced with Cyble). Hits if any of the 36 SHA256s land on a managed endpoint via download, MDM sync staging directory, or arrive as an email attachment — covers the delivery stage for organisations with BYOD that touches corporate mail/file infra. Rationale: 36 SHA256 hashes published by ESET, with the family corroborated by Cyble (https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/), Malpedia (apk.btmob entry), and Infosecurity Magazine. Hash-IOC matches are unambiguous when they hit — main delivery vectors for corporate exposure are (a) APKs reaching mail attachments destined for company-issued Android devices, and (b) APKs landing in a Windows download folder before sideload to a paired Android device. Includes ImFileEvent for Sentinel cross-vendor portability. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/btmob-android-rat-maas-builder/ • https://www.scworld.com/brief/btmob-android-rat-poses-significant-threat-with-easy-to-use-builder
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002 T1474.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Email.Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TI/RE analyst intentionally staging a known BTMOB sample on a sandbox host
  • AV/EDR signature-update package that ships hashes (rare — most vendors deliver hashes via signed catalog, not as raw files)
  • MDM / mobile-AV scanning hub that pulls APK samples for offline analysis
  • Penetration-testing lab building a knowledge base of public Android samples
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB" and DeviceName !startswith "MALW-RE" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("sandbox-svc","ti-analyst","detonation-svc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm hostname is NOT in the TI/RE allowlist; pull FileOriginUrl and the email NetworkMessageId — if origin is a webmail attachment or fake-store URL, treat as live phishing. Identify the user and check for prior UrlClickEvents to BTMOB phishing themes (streaming, crypto-mining, LATAM tax/customs lures). 2) Contain: quarantine the file via Defender 'Stop and quarantine'; if the recipient is on managed Android, push MDM device-quarantine and revoke the user's SSO/MFA sessions; block the FileOriginUrl domain at proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot the SHA256 across the org via DeviceFileEvents/EmailAttachmentInfo for additional recipients; sweep network telemetry for arbsniper.com and the BTMOB hosted-IP cluster (see sibling UCs); check whether the user's Android device beaconed to those C2s in DeviceNetworkEvents from corporate WiFi.

title: BTMOB Android RAT APK SHA256 Sighting

Egress to BTMOB hosted C2 cluster (LATAM/Hetzner IPs, Google CDN excluded) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate-network egress to the BTMOB C2 hosting footprint published by ESET, scoped to the non-CDN subset (Hetzner 178.156.x, LATAM bulletproof 191.96.x / 191.101.x / 200.9.x / 78.135.x / 79.133.x, Cloudflare front 104.21.64.137, 195.160.221.203). The Google IPs in ESET's IOC list are intentionally excluded because they are Google CDN ranges that would FP on every browser session. Rationale: Excludes the Google CDN ranges (74.125.x, 142.251.x, 173.194.x, 192.178.x) from ESET's IOC list which would generate overwhelming FPs on every browser session — these are Google services arbsniper.com / BTMOB happens to use for tracking/analytics, not C2. Focuses on the genuine BTMOB hosting footprint: Hetzner (178.156.x), LATAM bulletproof clusters (191.96.x, 191.101.x, 200.9.x), and the Cloudflare front (104.21.64.137). Hunting tier because the LATAM hosts may serve other tenants. Cyble's Feb 2025 write-up corroborates the LATAM C2 pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://cyble.com/blog/btmob-rat-newly-discovered-android-malware/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/apk.btmob
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate LATAM e-commerce / payments traffic to the 191.96.x.x bulletproof-hosting neighbour tenants (these IPs serve many low-reputation sites)
  • Cloudflare edge IP 104.21.64.137 being assigned to a benign customer domain after BTMOB rotated off — Cloudflare IPs are shared
  • Internet-scanning / threat-research traffic from a vuln-scanner that walks IP space
  • Travel-laptop user on LATAM hotel WiFi NATed through a shared address that happens to share a /24 with a flagged host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") or RemotePort !in (80, 443) | where DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("vuln-scanner","recon-svc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: enrich the RemoteIP with current passive DNS / Cloudflare reverse lookup — if PTR is now a clearly legitimate brand, downrate. For 104.21.64.137, check the HTTP Host header (proxy log) — if it's not arbsniper.com or an obvious lure domain, it's a Cloudflare neighbour and benign. 2) Contain: if the InitiatingProcessFileName is a corporate browser AND the connection went to the 191.96.x cluster, block the destination at the firewall and check the user for the BTMOB phishing lure in mail; if it's a non-browser process with no business case, isolate the host via Defender Live Response. 3) Hunt: pivot the user/host into the arbsniper.com UC and BTMOB APK SHA256 UC; check DeviceFileEvents for any newly-dropped APK or Android-emulator install (BlueStacks/NoxPlayer paired with these C2 calls would indicate desktop-side device-pairing test of a BTMOB build).
let LookbackDays = 30d;
let BtmobC2 = dynamic([

  "191.96.79.133", "191.96.79.179", "191.96.79.41", "200.9.155.153",

]);

| order by LastSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high

CISA KEV: CVE-2026-48172 — LiteSpeed cPanel Plugin Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

CISA KEV
2026-05-26 1 use case 0 techniques 2 kill-chain phases detected

LiteSpeed cPanel Plugin contains privilege escalation vulnerability that is exposed via the user-end cPanel plugin, which can be abused by any cPanel user account to execute arbitrary scripts with root privileges. Vendor: LiteSpeed, Product: cPanel Plugin. Federal patch due: 2026-05-29.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised laravel-lang Composer package: helpers.php in vendor tree
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Laravel Lang Supply Chain Advisory
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Laravel-Lang stealer file drop in .laravel_locale temp directory · [LLM] DebugChromium.exe execution (Laravel-Lang stealer Windows artifact) · [LLM] cscript/wscript executing a script from .laravel_locale temp directory · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Laravel-Lang supply chain C2/exfil to flipboxstudio.info · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Laravel-Lang supply chain C2/exfil to flipboxstudio.info AICommand & Control High
Hunts DNS lookups, SNI, or HTTP host headers to flipboxstudio[.]info — the C2/exfil domain used by the May 2026 Laravel-Lang Composer package compromise. The domain hosts both /payload (second-stage) and /exfil (stolen secrets), so any traffic to it from a Laravel-running host or CI runner indicates active compromise. Rationale: flipboxstudio[.]info is the single attacker-controlled C2/exfil endpoint named in the Snyk advisory and corroborated by StepSecurity, The Hacker News, Socket and Cyberpress. The domain has no legitimate use, so any successful resolution or connection is high-fidelity. Hits both DNS and HTTP/SNI telemetry to catch the resolution even if the payload connection is blocked. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/laravel-lang-php-packages-compromised.html • https://socket.dev/blog/laravel-lang-compromise • https://github.com/Laravel-Lang/http-statuses/issues/277
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1195.002
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution Network_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel feed ingestion tools or sandbox detonators resolving the IOC for enrichment (e.g. urlscan.io workers, VirusTotal retrohunts)
  • Security researchers manually browsing the indicator from a corporate workstation
  • Brand-protection / takedown vendors fetching the domain for evidence
  • DNS sinkhole or honeypot infrastructure replaying the IOC
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("urlscan-worker.exe","vt-fetch.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("threat-intel-svc","sandbox-detonator")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the resolving host and the initiating process; pull DeviceProcessEvents for the same DeviceId at ±10min to see if PHP (php-fpm, php.exe, artisan, composer) or cscript.exe is the parent. If the host runs Laravel, treat as confirmed. 2) Contain: sinkhole flipboxstudio[.]info at egress proxy/DNS, isolate the host with EDR, rotate every credential that ever touched it (AWS/GCP/Azure profile files, kubeconfigs, Vault tokens, CI/CD tokens, SSH keys, .env values, browser-stored creds, password vaults, crypto wallets, Slack/Discord/Telegram tokens). 3) Hunt: enumerate every project's composer.lock for laravel-lang/lang, laravel-lang/http-statuses, laravel-lang/attributes, laravel-lang/actions; cross-reference with UC5 file-hunt; review egress logs for the domain across all CI/CD runners and staging environments.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "flipboxstudio.info" or RemoteUrl endswith "flipboxstudio.info"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="DnsEvents", Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has "flipboxstudio.info" or RequestURL has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="CommonSecurityLog", Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Name=DestinationHostName, QueryType=RequestMethod, ResultCode=tostring(EventOutcome)),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has "flipboxstudio.info"
  | project TimeGenerated, Source="ImDnsActivity", Computer=SrcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Name=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, ResultCode=DnsResponseCodeName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Laravel-Lang stealer file drop in .laravel_locale temp directory AIInstallation High
Hunts file creation under any .laravel_locale subdirectory of a temp path. The Snyk advisory documents three artifacts under <tmp>/.laravel_locale/: an md5-hashed infection marker, a 12-hex-char .php second-stage stealer, and (on Windows) an 8-hex-char .vbs launcher. The directory name is unique to this campaign and has no benign use. Rationale: The Snyk IOC table explicitly names <tmp>/.laravel_locale/<md5>, <tmp>/.laravel_locale/<12 hex>.php, and <tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 hex>.vbs as stealer artifacts; StepSecurity corroborates the /tmp staging behaviour. The directory string is unique to this campaign and matches regardless of whether tmp resolves to /tmp, $TMPDIR, or %TEMP%. The filename regex extensions tag which stage fired for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack • https://socket.dev/blog/laravel-lang-compromise
ATT&CKT1059 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate package or internal tool coincidentally named .laravel_locale (none known)
  • DFIR analyst staging recovered artifacts into a folder for analysis
  • Backup software restoring a previously-infected host's temp directory
  • Container image build caching a directory of that name
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup-restore.exe","veeam.backup.shell.exe","7z.exe","tar.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("restore","extract","unzip"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the directory contents and the InitiatingProcessFileName/CommandLine — expect php (php-fpm, php-cgi, php.exe, artisan, queue:work) as the writer. Hash any .php/.vbs found and look up against AlienVault/VT. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the writing process tree, preserve the directory for forensics before any cleanup script runs (the stealer self-deletes). Rotate all credentials reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessFileName + AccountName for all hosts that wrote .laravel_locale in the last 30d, then check each for outbound traffic to flipboxstudio[.]info (UC1) and presence of vendor/laravel-lang/*/src/helpers.php (UC5).

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has ".laravel_locale"
| extend Marker = iff(FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{32}$", "infection_marker", "")
| extend Stage2 = iff(FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{12}\.php$", "stealer_php", "")
| extend VbsLauncher = iff(FileName matches regex @"^[a-f0-9]{8}\.vbs$", "vbs_launcher", "")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, Marker, Stage2, VbsLauncher, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

DebugChromium.exe execution (Laravel-Lang stealer Windows artifact) AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of DebugChromium.exe anywhere on disk. The Snyk advisory names this binary as a Windows artifact observed on hosts infected by the Laravel-Lang Composer supply-chain stealer. The name impersonates a Chrome debug build to blend in with developer tooling; there is no legitimate Microsoft/Google binary by this name. Rationale: DebugChromium.exe is called out by name in the Snyk IOC table as a Windows artifact observed on infected hosts. The string is unique - no legitimate Microsoft or Google product ships a binary by this name - so a process-create on this filename is essentially confirmation of infection. Captures parent (likely cscript.exe from UC4) for chain reconstruction. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-advisory/ • https://securityonline.info/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack-rce-backdoor/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer naming a personal Chromium debug build DebugChromium.exe (uncommon — Chromium devs use chrome.exe or content_shell.exe)
  • Red-team operator re-using the IOC name in an authorised exercise
  • Threat-intel sandbox detonating the sample on a corporate analyst VM
Response runbook
1) Triage: collect SHA256 of the image and compare against the StepSecurity/Snyk hash list. Identify parent — UC4 will show cscript.exe from %TEMP%\.laravel_locale as the spawner. Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the same DeviceId to confirm UC1 traffic. 2) Contain: isolate host with EDR, kill the process tree, quarantine the binary, rotate every credential cached or used on the host. 3) Hunt: search the file across the fleet using SHA256 from the first hit (DeviceFileEvents), and pivot on InitiatingProcessParentFileName to find the originating Laravel/CI process.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "DebugChromium.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\DebugChromium.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, TokenElevationType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

cscript/wscript executing a script from .laravel_locale temp directory AIInstallation High
Hunts cscript.exe or wscript.exe invocations whose command line references a .laravel_locale path. The Snyk advisory describes the Windows execution chain as the malicious PHP helper writing an 8-hex-char .vbs into %TEMP%\.laravel_locale\ and launching it via cscript — pairing the canonical script interpreter with the stealer's unique staging directory yields a tight signal. Rationale: Snyk explicitly documents the Windows execution chain as a .vbs launcher under %TEMP%\.laravel_locale\. The compound (cscript|wscript) + .laravel_locale leaves no realistic benign matches — neither Windows nor any common dev tool stages scripts in a directory of that name. Captures parent process so triage shows the PHP runtime (php.exe / php-cgi) that originated the launch. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack • https://snyk.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-advisory/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1218 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR replay of recovered samples in a sandbox folder reusing the name
  • Red-team exercise replicating the IOC for control validation
  • Backup software temporarily extracting a previously-infected host into a similarly-named directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("backup-restore.exe","7z.exe","explorer.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("restore","extract","unzip"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture full CommandLine (the .vbs path will be embedded), the parent (expect php.exe / php-cgi.exe / artisan when fresh), and confirm InitiatingProcessParentFileName. Hash the .vbs from disk before the stealer self-deletes. 2) Contain: kill the cscript process tree, isolate the host, quarantine the .vbs and DebugChromium.exe (UC3). Rotate all credentials reachable from the host. 3) Hunt: pivot the parent process's user/host across DeviceFileEvents for vendor\laravel-lang\*\src\helpers.php (UC5) and DeviceNetworkEvents for flipboxstudio.info (UC1) to confirm the full chain.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("cscript.exe","wscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has ".laravel_locale"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688

Compromised laravel-lang Composer package: helpers.php in vendor tree AIDelivery High
Hunts the file write or presence of src/helpers.php under vendor/laravel-lang/{lang,http-statuses,attributes,actions}/. A legitimate localization package has no reason to ship an autoload-files helper, so any host whose Composer cache contains this file pulled a poisoned tag during the May 22-23 2026 incident and should be treated as compromised until the package is rolled back and credentials rotated. Rationale: The Snyk detection guidance explicitly tells defenders to inspect vendor/laravel-lang/*/ for the presence of src/helpers.php — legitimate releases of these four localization packages do not ship a helpers file or use autoload.files. The package-name regex narrows to the four named-compromised packages (lang, http-statuses, attributes, actions) per the affected-versions table, avoiding stray matches on other laravel-lang/* repos. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/Laravel-Lang/http-statuses/issues/277 • https://gbhackers.com/compromise-laravel-lang-packages/ • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/laravel-lang-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic image mount where an analyst is reviewing a known-compromised host's vendor tree
  • Repo of pinned/known-bad samples kept for red-team or detection-engineering validation
  • Backup-restore of an older Laravel project that legitimately had a custom helpers.php (rare — the path /vendor/laravel-lang/<pkg>/src/ is vendor-managed, devs shouldn't write there)
  • Internal fork of a laravel-lang package that genuinely adds a helpers file (audit composer.json autoload.files to confirm intent)
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the actual helpers.php content and composer.json on the host — confirm autoload.files registers it and the contents include an HTTP fetch to flipboxstudio[.]info. Pull composer.lock to record the exact poisoned version+integrity hash. 2) Contain: roll back to a known-good pinned version after Packagist relists (or vendor a clean local fork), invalidate Composer cache (composer clearcache + delete vendor/), rebuild and redeploy. Rotate every credential the affected runtime could have touched: AWS/GCP/Azure profiles, kubeconfigs, Vault tokens, CI/CD secrets, SSH keys, .env values, browser sessions, password manager vaults, crypto wallets, Slack/Discord/Telegram tokens. 3) Hunt: chain to UC1 (flipboxstudio.info egress) and UC2 (.laravel_locale temp drops) on the same DeviceId/runner to determine if the second-stage actually executed and exfiltrated. Search every CI/CD job log and container image registry for vendor/laravel-lang/*/src/helpers.php to find untracked compromis
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "vendor\\laravel-lang\\" or FolderPath has "vendor/laravel-lang/"
| where FileName =~ "helpers.php"
| extend Package = extract(@"laravel-lang[\\/](lang|http-statuses|attributes|actions)", 1, FolderPath)
| where isnotempty(Package)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, Package, SHA256, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "vendor/laravel-lang/" or TargetFilePath has @"vendor\laravel-lang\"
| where TargetFileName =~ "helpers.php"
| extend Package = extract(@"laravel-lang[\\/](lang|http-statuses|attributes|actions)", 1, TargetFilePath)
| where isnotempty(Package)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, Package, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)

| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc

| order by ConnCount desc

| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

            - '\pwsh.exe'

            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the

level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375") or SHA1 in~ ("bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375") or MD5 in~ ("bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375") or SHA1 in~ ("bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375") or MD5 in~ ("bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["bba2e443dc7ff1f8704f52a5375383e3f4f643b8", "a5ea2e8fa92ccf29cdb1d2dadbeb27722b2bff37", "556d2b335d4d6d92139822017ee461b668afe375"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Composer install of malicious helpers.php in laravel-lang vendor package
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Supply Chain Attack Targets Laravel-Lang Packages with Credential Stealer
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] cscript.exe launching .vbs from .laravel_locale temp directory · [LLM] Stealer or VBS launcher dropped into .laravel_locale temp directory · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 egress to flipboxstudio.info from Laravel-Lang composer dropper · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

C2 egress to flipboxstudio.info from Laravel-Lang composer dropper AICommand & Control High
Detects any HTTP/DNS contact with the hard-coded C2 domain flipboxstudio.info (decoded from integer array in the malicious src/helpers.php). Both the /payload fetch (stage-2 stealer download) and /exfil (AES-256 encrypted credential exfil) hit the same FQDN, so any resolution or connection is unambiguously malicious. Rationale: Anchored on the article's named C2 domain flipboxstudio.info plus the /payload and /exfil URL paths quoted verbatim. Corroborated by https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities and https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/malicious-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities/

  • Aikido/Snyk/Socket scanning engine on a build agent verifying the IOC
  • Legacy reference to defunct flipboxstudio brand if same FQDN was previously legitimate (verify WHOIS dates)

| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("aikido-scanner.exe","socket-cli.exe","snyk.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--threat-intel","--ioc-validate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on DeviceName/SourceIP — pull the initiating process. If parent is php.exe/php-fpm/composer or cscript.exe with .laravel_locale path, treat as confirmed dropper detonation. 2) Contain: block flipboxstudio.info at proxy/DNS firewall org-wide; isolate the host; preserve <tmp>/.laravel_locale/* for forensics before any cleanup. 3) Hunt: grep all PHP project vendor/ directories for vendor/laravel-lang/*/src/helpers.php; check composer.lock for laravel-lang/lang, /attributes, /http-statuses pinned in the affected 233 versions; rotate ALL credentials within reach of the affected host (AWS, GCP, Azure, kubeconfig, SSH, .git-credentials, browser saved passwords, crypto wallet seeds).

| order by Timestamp desc

cscript.exe launching .vbs from .laravel_locale temp directory AIInstallation High
Detects the Windows arm of the Laravel-Lang dropper: the malicious src/helpers.php writes an 8-hex-character .vbs launcher into <temp>\.laravel_locale\ and executes it silently via cscript. Process tree is php/php-fpm/php-cgi (or anything that triggered composer autoload) → cscript.exe with a .vbs path containing `.laravel_locale`. Rationale: Anchored on two article-quoted strings together: `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 random hex chars>.vbs` and the explicit `runs the payload silently via cscript` Windows-launcher behaviour. The 8-hex regex makes this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/
ATT&CKT1059.005 T1105 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer reproducing the IOC in a sandbox (would show non-php parent)
  • Security tool / sandbox detonating sample with reused .laravel_locale path naming
  • Internal red-team exercise replaying the dropper
  • Unrelated legitimate VBS in a folder coincidentally containing the substring '.laravel_locale' (extremely unlikely given path-component anchoring)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full process tree — confirm parent is php.exe / php-cgi.exe / php-fpm / composer.phar / cmd spawning composer; capture SHA256 of the .vbs and any dropped .php in same dir. 2) Contain: kill cscript chain, isolate host, snapshot <tmp>\.laravel_locale\ for forensics, block flipboxstudio.info. 3) Hunt: cross-reference DeviceFileEvents for any .php files written to .laravel_locale on this host (the 5,900-line stealer), enumerate cloud/SSH/browser/crypto creds present on the host and rotate immediately; pivot to other dev workstations with same composer.lock entries for laravel-lang/lang/attributes/http-statuses.
let LookbackDays = 14d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where FileName =~ "cscript.exe" or FileName =~ "wscript.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @".laravel_locale"
   and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd   = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage  = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd    = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
union isfuzzy=true
(
  SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "\\cscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\wscript.exe"
  | where CommandLine has ".laravel_locale" and CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.laravel_locale[\\\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
),
(
  ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where ActingProcessName endswith "cscript.exe" or ActingProcessName endswith "wscript.exe"
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has ".laravel_locale"
     and ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\.laravel_locale[\\\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Composer install of malicious helpers.php in laravel-lang vendor package AIDelivery Medium
Detects composer (or any file mover) writing a src/helpers.php file under vendor/laravel-lang/{lang,attributes,http-statuses}/ — the article confirms this file does not exist in the legitimate packages and was injected by the attacker via fork-tag commits. Catches the supply-chain payload at composer-install time, before the dropper detonates. Rationale: Anchored on the article-quoted file name (`src/helpers.php`) plus the three affected package names verbatim (`laravel-lang/lang`, `laravel-lang/attributes`, `laravel-lang/http-statuses`). The file is novel to the malicious tags, so any write is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://thehackernews.com/2026/03/fake-laravel-packages-on-packagist.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer re-pulling a cleaned/patched laravel-lang version that legitimately ships helpers.php in a future release
  • Forensic restore of a known-bad artifact from backup for IR analysis
  • Composer cache deduplication tools copying the file between projects
  • Container-image rebuild that includes a pinned malicious version still present in composer.lock
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process (expect composer.phar / php composer / docker build / CI runner). Pull SHA256 of the dropped helpers.php and search for the strings `laravel_lang_locale`, `laravel_lang_fallback`, `flipboxstudio` or integer-array C2 encoding inside the file. 2) Contain: delete the vendor/laravel-lang/ directory; pin composer.json to a known-good pre-attack version (or remove these packages entirely); re-run composer install; block flipboxstudio.info at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: if the file appears, treat the host as compromised — rotate every credential reachable from it (AWS/GCP/Azure keys, EC2 IMDS role, kubeconfig, SSH keys, .git-credentials, GitHub/GitLab CLI tokens, browser saved passwords, crypto wallet seeds, Slack/Discord/Telegram bot tokens, VPN creds); pivot to all other workstations/CI runners sharing the same composer.lock.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 30d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "helpers.php"
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)[\\\\/]vendor[\\\\/]laravel-lang[\\\\/](lang|attributes|http-statuses)[\\\\/]src[\\\\/]helpers\.php$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256

Stealer or VBS launcher dropped into .laravel_locale temp directory AIInstallation High
Detects file creation inside <temp>\.laravel_locale\ matching the article's exact naming patterns: 12-hex-character .php (the ~5,900-line stealer fetched from flipboxstudio.info/payload) or 8-hex-character .vbs (Windows cscript launcher). Catches the runtime dropper post-detonation, including the marker MD5 file that gates re-execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim path patterns: `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<md5_hash>` (32-hex marker), `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<12 random hex chars>.php` (stealer body), `<tmp>/.laravel_locale/<8 random hex chars>.vbs` (Windows launcher). The directory name plus the hex-only filename regex makes near-zero-FP. Cross-checked with https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities • https://gbhackers.com/malicious-laravel-packages/
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005 T1140
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Forensic tool unpacking a captured sample preserving original directory name
  • Aikido / Socket / Snyk sandbox detonating the IOC on a build agent
  • Security researcher reproducing the dropper for analysis
  • Backup restore of a previously infected host that contains residual .laravel_locale artifacts
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm initiating process is php / cscript / wscript / curl / wget — if so the dropper is mid-execution. Capture SHA256 of every file under .laravel_locale and submit to VT/IR sandbox; preserve the .vbs and .php contents to identify which of the 15 stealer modules ran (cloud-creds vs crypto-wallet vs browser-saved-passwords). 2) Contain: kill the cscript/php process tree, isolate host, block flipboxstudio.info DNS/IP, snapshot disk before remediation since the stealer self-deletes. 3) Hunt: assume credential theft completed — rotate every credential the article enumerates (AWS keys + IMDS role, GCP ADC, Azure MSAL cache, DO/Heroku/Vercel/Netlify/Railway/Fly tokens, kubeconfigs, Vault tokens, all SSH keys, .git-credentials, .npmrc/.pypirc/.composer/auth.json, GitHub/GitLab CLI tokens, Slack/Discord/Telegram bot tokens, browser saved passwords across 17 Chromium browsers + Firefox + KeePass + 1Password + Bitwarden, all crypto wallets and seed phrases). Audit AWS CloudTrail / 
let LookbackDays = 14d;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has @".laravel_locale" or FolderPath has @"/.laravel_locale/" or FolderPath has @"\\.laravel_locale\\"
| where (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$")
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$")
     or (FileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 14d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath has ".laravel_locale"
| where (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$")
     or (TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Laravel-Lang Stealer Files Dropped in .laravel_locale Temp Dir
id: 1c8a6e4d-3f72-49bc-9d18-7a2bf0c4e5e9
description: Detects creation of files inside <temp>\.laravel_locale\ matching the Laravel-Lang stealer payload pattern (12-hex .php, 8-hex .vbs, or 32-hex MD5 marker file). Article (Aikido, 22 May 2026) confirms the dropper writes these exact patterns to the system temp directory.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/supply-chain-attack-targets-laravel-lang-packages-with-credential-stealer
  - https://socket.dev/blog/malicious-packagist-packages-disguised-as-laravel-utilities
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/23
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1105
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_dir:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\.laravel_locale\'
      - '/.laravel_locale/'
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|re|i:
      - '\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{12}\.php$'
      - '\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$'
      - '\.laravel_locale[\\/][0-9a-f]{32}$'
  condition: selection_dir and selection_name
falsepositives:
  - None expected; folder name is attacker-specific
level: critical
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\.laravel_locale\\* OR */.laravel_locale/*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @file.path:(*/.laravel_locale/*)) OR (source:windows.defender @FilePath:(*\\.laravel_locale\\* OR */.laravel_locale/*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/]/i
| (TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/][0-9a-f]{12}\.php$/i or TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/][0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$/i or TargetFileName=/[\\\/]\.laravel_locale[\\\/][0-9a-f]{32}$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.laravel_locale\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.laravel_locale/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user values(Filesystem.file_path) as paths from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.laravel_locale\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/.laravel_locale/*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.action
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{12}\.php$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{8}\.vbs$") OR match(file_name, "(?i)^[0-9a-f]{32}$")
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/

date: 2026/05/02

            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'

| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"

Nezha CVE-2026-46716 exploit: POST /api/v1/cron with empty servers + CronCoverAll AIExploitation High
Detects the exploit signature for Nezha Monitoring CVE-2026-46716 where a RoleMember submits a cron task with `cover=1` (CronCoverAll) and `servers=[]` to trigger the vacuous-true permission bypass in createCron. Targets the dashboard's web tier via reverse-proxy / WAF / IIS / App Service logs that capture POST bodies or at least the URI. Rationale: Targets the exact URI named in the GHSA advisory (`POST /api/v1/cron` gated by commonHandler not adminHandler) and the body shape that triggers the vacuous-true bypass (`servers=[]` + `cover=1`). The endpoint is rare under normal operation — admins create cron tasks occasionally, so even the URI alone is a strong pivot; body inspection (when WAF/proxy logs include it) elevates to deterministic. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-99gv-2m7h-3hh9 • https://github.com/nezhahq/nezha • https://nezha.wiki/en_US/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078 T1068
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Nezha admin (RoleAdmin) creating a legitimate cron task during scheduled-job onboarding
  • Infrastructure-as-code tooling (Terraform/Ansible) provisioning monitoring jobs via the dashboard API
  • Automated CI pipeline using a stored admin token to upsert cron tasks for canary checks
  • Penetration-test / red-team validation of this exact CVE on a non-production dashboard
Suppression filter
// Add allow-list for known admin source IPs and CI service principals
| where SrcIP !in ("<admin-bastion-ip>", "<ci-runner-cidr>")
| where SourceUserName !in~ ("admin", "ci-bot", "terraform")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the source IP and UPN/JWT subject from the request; check whether the actor's role is RoleMember (Role==1) — anything other than RoleAdmin is exploit-confirmed. Inspect body for `"servers":[]` and `"cover":1` if logged. 2) Contain: Block the source IP at the perimeter; revoke the offending account's JWT (force-logout) and disable the user record. If OAuth2 self-bind is enabled, temporarily disable new-user OAuth registration. Patch the dashboard to a commit after 50dc8e6 (cron routes moved to adminHandler) or apply the upstream fix. 3) Hunt: Enumerate `cron` table on the dashboard DB for entries where `user_id != admin` and `cover=1` AND `servers IS NULL/empty`; pull the `command` field of each to assess what ran. Check `notification` and `notification_group` tables for member-owned webhooks pointing to external URLs. Then pivot to UC2/UC3 on every monitored host that received the task.
// Primary: WAF / proxy logs that capture request body in DeviceCustomString or RequestContext
let ExploitBodyPattern = @'(?is)"servers"\s*:\s*\[\s*\][^}]*"cover"\s*:\s*1|"cover"\s*:\s*1[^}]*"servers"\s*:\s*\[\s*\]';
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL endswith "/api/v1/cron"
| extend Body = strcat(coalesce(DeviceCustomString1, ""), " ", coalesce(DeviceCustomString2, ""), " ", coalesce(DeviceCustomString3, ""), " ", coalesce(RequestContext, ""), " ", coalesce(Message, ""))
| where Body matches regex ExploitBodyPattern or RequestURL has "cover=1"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=SourceIP, Dst=DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, Body, RequestClientApplication, SourceUserName),
(W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem endswith "/api/v1/cron"
| where scStatus >= 200 and scStatus < 300
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=cIP, Dst=Computer, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserName, csUserAgent, scStatus),
(AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where CsUriStem endswith "/api/v1/cron"
| where ScStatus >= 200 and ScStatus < 300
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIP=CIp, Dst=CsHost, CsUriStem, CsUriQuery, CsUsername, UserAgent, ScStatus)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
